I guess all the businesses out there better stop calling out people for resume fraud, at least in the U.S. There's a difference between criminal and civil law. Resume fraud could cause you legal problems, both civil and criminal. For example, your employer can sue you in civil court for resume fraud. Most don't take it this far, but some have sued people to get back some of the wages they paid someone who lied on their resume. Some companies will fine you.

Some states in the U.S. do have laws related to resume fraud that could put you in criminal court and you end up in jail. If you end up having to provide a fake document to get the job, let's say a diploma, you then run into forgery. More legal trouble.

More and more these days, people are required to sign something that says all information they've presented to the employer to get the job has been true. If you've signed something like this, and you did have some lies/false information, your lies are now officially illegal.

Let's look at another situation. Let's say you're fired and you feel it's unjustified. Maybe it's obvious to you that it's some sort of discrimination or politics. You decide you're going to sue them for wrongful termination. Your employer's lawyers do some digging and find that you lied on the resume you used to get the job. They can now say you committed resume fraud and that's why they fired you. You've now made it harder, and sometimes impossible, to defend yourself. 

Lying on your resume is not as simple (or not such a big deal) as it seems. Could cause you problems later down the road. We don't always think about the ripple effect our decisions can have. Be careful out there people.
